### Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development and opportunity around the world. The quality of education among a country's population is one of the most prominent indicators of the current wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies widely across different places and groups of people. I'm curious about the extent of these differences, so I turned to the data to find out.

I used data from the United Nations' Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program; I obtained data from [UNDP's open database](https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/documentation-and-downloads) that covers 34 years: 1990 to 2023. Note that the variables that I was interested in were missing data past 2023 so the past couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren't included in this analysis.

The data contains information on countries' adult population, defined as people over 25 for the metrics I'm interested in, and specifically their average amount of education that they've obtained by then. There are also more variables providing breakdowns by demographics, such as the same metrics split by gender as well as indicators of the country's economic level of development in the form of the GNI (Gross National Income) of the residents. These provide extra quantitative context on a country. TODO: There are also global metrics for each country equivalent.

```{r include = FALSE}
# Loading packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(gghighlight)
library(ggrepel)
library(countrycode)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rnaturalearthdata)
library(corrplot)

# Preparing the data
data <- read_excel("hdr-data.xlsx") %>%
  select(-c(yearStr, indexCode, index, dimension, note)) %>%
  mutate((across(c(year, value, actualValue), as.numeric)),
         continent = countrycode(countryIsoCode,
                                 origin = "iso3c",
                                 destination = "continent"),
         # NRO is for Naoero, a country in Oceania
         # ZZK.WORLD means the global value
         continent = ifelse(countryIsoCode == "NRO", "Oceania", continent))

# TODO: check for missing values
```

### Viewing the global level of education over time

In this initial plot of the average amount of education worldwide in years, it's clear that the world is gradually becoming more educated as a whole.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "",
       title = "The Average Amount of Education That Adults* Have (1990-2023)",
       caption = "*Adults 25+") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14))

# Calculating the average change in MYS per year

mys_1990 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 1990) %>%
  pull(actualValue)

mys_2023 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 2023) %>%
  pull(actualValue)
```

The world's education level in general has been steadily growing for the past 3 decades from ~`r round(mys_1990, 1)` years in 1990 to ~`r round(mys_1990, 1)` years in 2023 (a change of ~`r round(mys_2023 - mys_1990, 1)` years!), which is really nice to see. In fact, it has increased every single year, by ~`r round((mys_2023 - mys_1990) / (2023 - 1990), 1)` years each year.

However, if we look into how the level of education varies demographically and geographically, some disparities emerge.

### Exploring differences by gender

In this plot, when the metric is split by gender, a gap emerges.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by gender over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  mutate(indicatorCode = recode(indicatorCode,
                                "mys_f" = "Females",
                                "mys_m" = "Males")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, color = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Males" = "royalblue2",
                                "Females" = "violetred1")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "",
       title = "The Average Amount of Education That Adults Have (1990-2023)",
       colour = "") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9))
```

The average amount of education for females has never been more than for males. Although they've been increasing at very similar speeds — the lines are nearly parallel — there has consistently been a gap of around a year between them. Nonetheless, over the past few years, beginning in 2020, that gap has been shrinking. TODO: explain this table and mention that it only includes every 5 years until it's 2023.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"), is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(gender_gap = round(mys_m - mys_f, 1)) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023)) %>%
  select(year, gender_gap) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = gender_gap) %>%
  # Styling the table
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Educational Gender Gaps Across the Years") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

Another way to look at the gender gap is through the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education; secondary education, under the [UN's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)](https://www.uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2025/08/EDS-3-ISCED-Final-WEB.pdf), is an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the percentage of people who have secondary education by gender over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("se_m" = "royalblue2", "se_f" = "violetred1"),
                    labels = c("se_m" = "Males", "se_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "",
       title = "The Percentage of Adults With Secondary Education (1990-2023)",
       fill = "") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))
```

Again, the percentage of females with education worldwide has never exceeded the percentage of males, with a consistent difference of ~10%, but this has shrunk to around 8.2% in 2023.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"), is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(gender_gap = se_m - se_f, 1) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023)) %>%
  select(year, gender_gap) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = gender_gap) %>%
  # Styling the table
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Educational Gender Gaps Across the Years") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

### Exploring differences by location

Below is a graph of each continent's average amount of education of its population who are over 25 years old.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by continent over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_mys = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_mys, colour = continent)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "",
       title = "The Average Amount of Education That Adults Have (1990-2023)",
       colour = "Continent") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14))
```

Here are the top 5 countries in 2023, again in terms of the average time spent in education of the portion of its population who are over 25.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Making a table of the most educated countries in 2023
data %>%
  filter(year == 2023, indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  arrange(desc(actualValue)) %>%
  select(country, actualValue) %>%
  head(n = 5) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(country = "Country", actualValue = "Mean Years of Education") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Most Educated Countries (2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(column_labels.background.color = "#F9E076")
```

And here are the bottom 20. I'm including more rows in this table because the lower end of the range is more telling/revealing than the upper end.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Making a table of the least educated countries in 2023
data %>%
  filter(year == 2023, indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  arrange(actualValue) %>%
  select(country, actualValue) %>%
  head(n = 20) %>%
  mutate(difference_from_world = actualValue - mys_2023) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(country = "Country",
             actualValue = "Mean Years of Education",
             difference_from_world = "Distance From the World Average") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Least Educated Countries (2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(column_labels.background.color = "lightsteelblue2")
```

As for the countries that have been in the top 10 at least once for every year in the 34-year span... TODO: commentary

```{r include=FALSE}
# Making a table of the most educated countries (1990-2023)
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  # Ranking countries by the metric in ascending order
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  # Keeping only the top 10 for each year
  filter(rank >= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Counting how many times each country appeared in the bottom 10 across all years
  count(country, name = "times_in_top_10") %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_top_10)) %>%
  # Styling the table
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(country = "Country", times_in_top_10 = "# of Times in Top 10") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently High Education Rates") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(column_labels.background.color = "#F9E076")
```

Additionally, here is a table showing the countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, and the number of times it has been in the bottom 10. There are 17 countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, of which 4 countries (Afghanistan, Guinea, Mali, and Niger) have ranked in the bottom 10 in every year from 1990 to 2023.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Calculating the exact change between 1990 and 2023
changes <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", year %in% c(1990, 2023)) %>%
  select(country, year, actualValue) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year,
              values_from = actualValue,
              names_prefix = "value_") %>%
  mutate(change = value_2023 - value_1990)

# Making a table of the most educated countries (1990-2023)
# NOTE: I added are an extra 3 columns to show the change from 1990 to 2023
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(country, name = "times_in_bottom_10") %>%
  left_join(changes, by = "country") %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_bottom_10)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(country = "Country",
             times_in_bottom_10 = "# of Times in Bottom 10",
             value_1990 = "Mean Years of Education (1990)",
             value_2023 = "Mean Years of Education (2023)",
             change = "Change") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(value_1990, value_2023, change),
             decimals = 1) %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently Low Education Rates") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(column_labels.background.color = "lightsteelblue2")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
################################# RANDOM STUFF #################################

# Getting country boundaries
world <- ne_countries(scale = "small", returnclass = "sf")

# Assigning standardized continent names
world <- world %>%
  mutate(continent = countrycode(iso_a3, origin = "iso3c", destination = "continent"),
         region = countrycode(iso_a3, origin = "iso3c", destination = "region"),
         continent = case_when(continent == "Americas" & region %in%
                            c("Northern America", "Central America", "Caribbean") ~ "North America",
                          continent == "Americas" & region == "South America" ~ "South America",
                          TRUE ~ continent)) %>%
  filter(continent != "Antarctica")

# Preparing the data for mapping
new_data <- data %>%
  mutate(continent = countrycode(countryIsoCode, origin = "iso3c",
                                 destination = "continent"),
         region = countrycode(countryIsoCode, origin = "iso3c", destination = "region"),
         continent = case_when(continent == "Americas" & region %in%
                            c("Northern America", "Central America", "Caribbean") ~ "North America",
                          continent == "Americas" & region == "South America" ~ "South America",
                          TRUE ~ continent))

# Aggregating indicator data
continent_data <- new_data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

# Joining continent values to individual country geometries
map_dataset <- world %>%
  left_join(continent_data, by = "continent")

# Creating the map
ggplot(map_dataset) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = actualValue), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "Average Years of Education of Adults", low = "lightblue", high = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Value Distribution by Continent (2023)",
       subtitle = "SUBTITLE") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        legend.position = "bottom")

# Plotting a correlation matrix between some variables
# TODO: fix
colours <- colorRampPalette(c("#BB4444", "#EE9988", "#FFFFFF", "#77AADD", "#4477AA"))
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("gnipc", "hdi_rank", "mys", "ineq_edu"),
         !is.na(continent),
         year == 2023) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(countryIsoCode, continent, year),
              names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue) %>%
  select(where(is.numeric), -c(year)) %>%
  cor(method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>%
  corrplot(method = "color", type = "upper", col = colours(200),

           tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45)
```
